overview.title: ConvNet input shape and model.summary() of the first ConvNet
overview.main_topic: The (height, width, channels) input convention, Listing 8.2's model summary with output shapes and parameter counts, and the channels-last versus channels-first sidebar.
overview.central_idea: A ConvNet consumes rank-3 image tensors (height, width, channels), excluding the batch axis. As data passes through Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layers, height and width shrink while the number of channels, set by each Conv2D's filters argument, grows. Keras defaults to channels-last; channels-first is a configurable convention.
overview.importance: Reading a model summary, predicting each layer's output shape and parameter count, is a core skill for designing ConvNets, and the channel-axis convention is a frequent source of bugs when moving between ecosystems.

summary:
The page explains what the ConvNet of Listing 8.1 consumes and produces. A ConvNet takes input tensors of shape `(image_height, image_width, image_channels)`, *not including the batch dimension*; for MNIST this is `(28, 28, 1)`.

**Listing 8.2** calls `model.summary()` on the model, named `"functional"`:

| Layer | Output shape | Params |
|---|---|---|
| input_layer | (None, 28, 28, 1) | 0 |
| conv2d | (None, 26, 26, 64) | 640 |
| max_pooling2d | (None, 13, 13, 64) | 0 |
| conv2d_1 | (None, 11, 11, 128) | 73,856 |
| max_pooling2d_1 | (None, 5, 5, 128) | 0 |
| conv2d_2 | (None, 3, 3, 256) | 295,168 |
| global_average_pooling2d | (None, 256) | 0 |
| dense | (None, 10) | 2,570 |

Total params: **372,234** (1.42 MB), all trainable. `None` is the batch axis of unknown size.

The authors point out that the output of every `Conv2D` and `MaxPooling2D` layer is a 3D tensor `(height, width, channels)`; **width and height shrink** deeper in the model, and the **number of channels is set by the first argument of `Conv2D`** (64, 128, 256).

The sidebar **Image data formats in deep learning frameworks** notes that some libraries, notably much of the PyTorch ecosystem, put channels first: `(channels, height, width)`. This is purely a convention and is configurable in Keras, globally with `keras.config.set_image_data_format("channels_first")` or per layer with the `data_format` argument of conv and pooling layers. Generally, keep the default unless you specifically need `"channels_first"`.

Beyond the book: the parameter counts follow from $(k^2 C_{in} + 1) C_{out}$ for a $k\times k$ convolution (see the math section), and the shapes from the valid 3x3 convolution shrinking each side by 2 and the 2x2 pooling halving it with rounding down.

paragraphs.what_it_says: ConvNet inputs are (image_height, image_width, image_channels), excluding the batch axis; for MNIST, (28, 28, 1).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each sample is a rank-3 tensor; a batch is rank 4, (batch, 28, 28, 1). Grayscale images have one channel, RGB images three.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Feeding the flattened (784,) MNIST vectors of chapter 2 to this model would fail; the data must be reshaped to (28, 28, 1).

terminology.meaning: The last axis of an image tensor: color components at the input (1 for grayscale) and learned feature maps deeper in the network.
The leading axis indexing samples; shown as None in the summary.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The summary lists each layer's output shape and parameter count; total 372,234 trainable parameters (1.42 MB).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Only Conv2D and Dense layers have weights. Pooling layers, the input layer and global average pooling have none. Most parameters sit in the deepest convolution (295,168), because its parameter count scales with input channels times output channels.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Lets you check that the model is wired as intended and estimate its size; 372,234 float32 parameters at 4 bytes each are about 1.42 MiB, matching the printed size.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Conv2D params = (k*k*C_in + 1) * C_out; Dense params = n_in * n_out + n_out.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Some libraries, notably much of the PyTorch ecosystem, use (channels, height, width) instead of (height, width, channels).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The same image can be stored with the channel axis first or last; models and data must agree on the convention.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Mixing conventions (e.g. loading channels-first data into a channels-last model) is a common source of shape errors or silent misinterpretation.

paragraphs.excerpt: This is purely a matter of convention, and in Keras is configurable.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Keras can switch convention globally with keras.config.set_image_data_format("channels_first") or per layer via data_format; usually keep the default.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The choice does not change what the model can learn; it only changes how tensors are laid out.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Knowing both switches helps when interoperating with channels-first data or pretrained code.

concepts.name: Image tensor (height, width, channels)
concepts.definition: The rank-3 per-sample representation of an image used by Keras ConvNets; batches add a leading axis.
concepts.intuition: A stack of 2-D grids, one per channel.
concepts.significance: Defines what every conv and pooling layer consumes and produces.
concepts.misconception: That the batch axis is part of keras.Input(shape=...); it is not.

concepts.name: Conv2D parameter count
concepts.definition: Number of trainable weights in a Conv2D layer: one k x k x C_in kernel plus one bias per output channel.
concepts.intuition: Each filter looks at every input channel over a small window; the count does not depend on image size.
concepts.significance: Explains why parameters concentrate in deep, wide conv layers.
concepts.misconception: That a larger image means more conv parameters; it only increases computation and output size.

concepts.name: channels_last vs channels_first
concepts.definition: Two conventions for where the channel axis goes in image tensors.
concepts.technical: Keras default channels_last; switch via keras.config.set_image_data_format or data_format per layer.
concepts.misconception: That one convention gives better models; the book says it is purely a matter of convention.

math.title: Parameter count of a Conv2D layer
math.source_text: Not printed as a formula; the counts 640, 73,856 and 295,168 appear in the Param # column of Listing 8.2.
math.operations: Multiply the kernel volume by the number of filters and add one bias per filter.
math.purpose: Reproduce and check the Param # column.
math.interpretation: Each filter has k*k*C_in weights; the count is independent of image size.
math.intuition: Parameters grow with the product of input and output channels, so later, wider layers dominate.

math.title: Output size of valid 3x3 convolution and 2x2 max pooling
math.source_text: Not printed as a formula; the shapes 28 -> 26 -> 13 -> 11 -> 5 -> 3 appear in the Output Shape column.

variables.meaning: Output height after convolution (stride 1, no padding) or after 2x2 pooling (stride 2).

math.operations: Subtract k-1 for convolution; halve and round down for pooling.
math.interpretation: A 3x3 window fits in H-2 positions per axis; 2x2 pooling keeps one value per 2x2 block.
math.intuition: Convolution trims the border; pooling downsamples.
math.numerical_example: $28 - 2 = 26$, $\lfloor 26/2 \rfloor = 13$, $13 - 2 = 11$, $\lfloor 11/2 \rfloor = 5$, $5 - 2 = 3$: exactly the sequence 28, 26, 13, 11, 5, 3 in the Output Shape column.

deeper.title: Where the parameters are
deeper.body: Beyond the book: of 372,234 parameters, about 79% (295,168) are in the last Conv2D, about 20% (73,856) in the second, and under 1% in the first conv and the classifier. Compare chapter 2's dense MNIST model, whose first Dense(512) layer alone had 784*512+512 = 401,920 parameters: the ConvNet is smaller yet, as p.256 promises, more accurate. Global average pooling helps by feeding only 256 values to the classifier instead of 3*3*256 = 2,304.

deeper.title: Converting between channel conventions
deeper.body: Beyond the book: with NumPy, `np.transpose(x, (0, 3, 1, 2))` turns a channels-last batch (N, H, W, C) into channels-first (N, C, H, W), and `(0, 2, 3, 1)` converts back. Use this when bringing data from a channels-first pipeline into a default Keras model.

misconceptions.correction: Height and width shrink, but channels grow (64, 128, 256) as set by the Conv2D filters argument.

takeaways: A Keras ConvNet takes (height, width, channels) inputs, without the batch axis; MNIST is (28, 28, 1).
Spatial size shrinks (28 -> 26 -> 13 -> 11 -> 5 -> 3) while channels grow (64 -> 128 -> 256).
The model has 372,234 trainable parameters; pooling layers have none.
Channel count is the first argument (filters) of Conv2D.
channels_first vs channels_last is a convention; Keras defaults to channels_last and can be switched globally or per layer.

questions.question: What is the output shape of max_pooling2d_1 in Listing 8.2?
questions.explanation: 2x2 pooling of 11x11 gives 5x5 (rounding down). 11x11 is the conv output before pooling, 6x6 would require rounding up, and 3x3x256 is the next conv.

questions.question: Verify the 73,856 parameters of conv2d_1.
questions.explanation: 3x3 kernels over 64 input channels, 128 filters, plus one bias each.

questions.question: Which argument of Conv2D controls the number of channels in its output?
questions.answer: The first argument, filters (64, 128 or 256 here).
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph after the summary.

questions.question: How can you make a single Keras conv layer use channels-first tensors?
questions.explanation: The sidebar names data_format per layer, or keras.config.set_image_data_format globally. Kernel reshaping or kernel_size changes are unrelated.

questions.question: If the input were (32, 32, 3) instead of (28, 28, 1), what would conv2d's output shape and parameter count be?
questions.explanation: Valid 3x3 convolution trims 2 per axis; parameters depend on input channels but not on image size.

questions.question: Why does the model's summary show None as the first dimension of every output shape?
questions.answer: It is the batch axis, whose size is not fixed when the model is defined.
questions.explanation: The input shape excludes the batch dimension; Keras adds it as None.

questions.question: Describe the general trend of tensor shapes through this ConvNet and why it is useful.
questions.answer: Height and width shrink while channel count grows: the network trades spatial resolution for more, richer features per location.
questions.explanation: The trend is stated on the page; the interpretation is an explanation beyond it.
